message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
# Points from "How We Work", from memory

The wording is mostly paraphrase. Phrases in quotation marks are ones I'm fairly confident are close to verbatim, but I may be wrong on details.

## Introduction
- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned
- Claims come from papers, colleagues, summaries, or your own earlier notes.
- A claim's weight comes partly from the evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Experience is one way a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- Conclusions from colleagues with years in an area have been tested in ways not visible on the page.
- When an experienced person states something with confidence, "that confidence is itself evidence": it reflects checks they've already made.
- A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and "quickly corrected by others." Understating is "more insidious": a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in work done well.
- **Example:** a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports the defect rate fell after a process change. Take it as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer
- Before responding, restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it.
- This is not politeness. It keeps the conversation moving rather than circling.
- The best reply starts from what you agree with: find what's right, say so, extend it.
- Replies that reopen settled points or lead with disagreement put people on the defensive and cost more time than they save.
- If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- A restatement is "the ground, not the contribution." The useful reply is the next step.
- **Example:** a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. The reply confirms the direction, acts on what can be done now, and says the budget will follow "in due course."

## 3. Go to the source
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks.
- Re-deriving a summary duplicates work and can signal you don't trust colleagues.
- A shared record lets the team build together. Members insisting on their own readings fragment the team into "private versions of the truth," and it stops being able to act.
- **Example:** a report is summarised as "costs fell 12%." Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the summary accurately.

## 4. Do not leave open what can be closed
- Mark which questions the evidence settles and which it leaves uncertain, then keep moving.
- Open questions have costs: they block decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When evidence leans clearly, record the lean as the working answer. It can be revisited; a question left hanging "tends to stay hanging."
- The mirror failure, keeping questions open because one more check feels safer, is "the more common one in careful people." It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- Once the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed.
- **Example:** a new form reduced errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Handle problems as they arise.

## 5. Help the colleague who sees differently
- New colleagues and people from other parts of the organisation see things differently. That's valuable only if their time goes where it's useful.
- A reviewer starting from scratch will mostly rediscover what the team already knows.
- When asking for a check, give context: what you've concluded, where you see risks, and what to focus on. A briefed reader finds issues faster.
- When you're the new reader, start from what others have concluded and read in that light.
- Raise objections when they're well-founded and the moment is right. Don't raise half-formed concerns in a meeting that has reached agreement. Take them to the person afterwards, once you're sure.

## 6. Make your moves where they will land well
- Before taking a step you think is good, check that it fits what the area's owners have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating, make the call once direction is confirmed, and release results when ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be redone, which costs more than a short conversation would have.
- Your view comes from your position; the owner sees considerations you can't. Asking first is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This isn't licence to wait indefinitely. Small routine steps need no sign-off, but for steps affecting others the default is to check first and then act together.
- **Example:** instead of restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether, and how, they'd like it restructured.

## 7. Failures come in pairs
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes towards the other.
- **Overclaiming / second-guessing:** overstating a provisional result; casting doubt on an established one.
- **Inventing a flaw / overlooking one:** finding a non-existent problem to look rigorous; missing a real one.
- **Closing too early / keeping open too long:** declaring an answer prematurely; refusing to accept the team's answer.
- **Abandoning a line / relitigating one:** dropping an agreed approach at the first difficulty; reopening a decided one.
- **Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively:** accepting anything; disputing what experienced colleagues have concluded.
- **Acting alone / waiting too long:** making calls others should have shaped; delaying steps already agreed.
- If you're correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- "When in doubt, remember that the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one."

## A last word
- The note isn't a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes careful work going well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team: experienced colleagues, shared records you can rely on, and an agreed direction.
- "Trust those. They are how good work gets done together."

## Where I'm unsure
- Whether Section 5 had its own worked example. I don't recall one.
- The exact order of the six pairs in Section 7.
